reason: E1 supports that oxygen contamination around 1 wt.% occurs and disrupts the single-phase solid solution, but it does not provide electrical conductivity data or evidence that such defects alter scattering. E2 shows simulated atomic-scale inhomogeneities at 300 K, yet it does not link these to conductivity or to the claimed temperature regimes. The key mechanistic premise—that these defects significantly affect conductivity and that modeling them improves predictions—lacks direct prior evidence from the cited passages.
premises: Oxygen contamination in HfNbTaTiZr can reach ~1 wt.% and prevents a single-phase random solid solution
Ab-initio simulations at 300 K indicate microstructural inhomogeneities (e.g., Ta-Nb clustering) in HfNbTaTiZr
Defects and oxygen-induced inhomogeneities create additional electron scattering centers
Ideal-crystal analytical models neglect these defect scattering contributions
Including defect scattering will improve conductivity prediction accuracy across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K
